1:
The resurrection narrative opens on a dated morning, a named woman and a moved stone, and Matthew Henry, the puritan-evangelical voice, explains at some length why it had to open on anything so checkable. There was no one thing, he says, of which the apostles were more concerned to produce substantial proof. Christ had appealed to his rising as the last and most cogent proof of his being Messiah, the sign of the prophet Jonah offered to those who would believe no other; and his enemies were correspondingly anxious to stifle the news, since if he were risen they were not merely murderers but murderers of the Messiah. The whole undertaking hung on it besides: if he gave his life a ransom and did not resume it, there is nothing to show the giving was accepted, and a surety imprisoned for our debt who lies there leaves us undone, as 1 Corinthians 15 says outright.

Henry then notices the strange economy of the evidence. He never showed himself alive to all the people, as Acts 10 concedes. We should have arranged it the other way, Henry admits — let the ignominious death be private and the glorious resurrection public — but God's thoughts are not ours, and the death was made public before the sun, which blushed and hid its face at it, while the proofs of the rising were kept back as a favour for particular friends, to be published by them so that those might be blessed who have not seen and yet have believed. The method satisfies anyone piously disposed to receive Christ's doctrine, and leaves room to object for anyone willingly ignorant, which Henry calls a fair trial suited to people still on probation. And the first step in the proof is simply this, that the grave was found empty: he is not here, and they must now tell us where he is, or we conclude him risen.

The grammatical-historical readers fix the time and the harmony. Robertson gives the idiom for the first day of the week that John shares with Mark 16 and Luke 24; Barnes sends the reader to Matthew 28 for the fuller account; Ellicott observes that John relates only the announcement of which he had special personal knowledge, each Gospel keeping the visit distinct from the angelic appearance. Clarke runs through the chapter's whole course by way of introduction — the empty tomb, the race of the two disciples, the vision of angels, the appearing to Mary.

Why only one woman is named is Henry's question too, and his answer is about her and not about John's sources. She was the most active and forward of them, and in her appeared the most affection — an affection kindled by consideration of what had been done for her, since much was forgiven her and therefore she loved much. She had attended his teaching and ministered to him of her own substance, as Luke 8 records, and had no business in Jerusalem but to wait on him, women being under no obligation to come up to the feast; knowing their Master would shortly be taken from their head, she followed the closer, as Elisha followed Elijah in 2 Kings 2. Love to Christ, Henry concludes, if it be cordial will be constant. Chrysostom had said the same thing more briefly: the Sabbath being over, during which it was unlawful to be there, she could rest no longer, but came very early to seek consolation at the grave. Calvin notes that the evangelists are the more careful to prove the rising because the hope of eternal life is extinguished without it, and that John accordingly collects many proofs — which is exactly what this verse begins to do.
2:
Mary does not wait at the tomb to reason about what she has seen. She runs, and the grammatical-historical readers catch the haste in the grammar itself: Robertson notes the vivid dramatic present, "runneth," and the indefinite plural of "they have taken away," a nobody and an everybody, exactly the shape of a suspicion that has no suspect. Mary fears a grave robbery, he says plainly; she has no idea of a resurrection. John, Robertson adds, deals only with Mary Magdalene, who left the tomb at once, before the other women and without seeing the angels whom Mark 16 and Matthew 28 report, while Luke 24 does not distinguish her separate errand from theirs at all.

Charles Ellicott presses the plural of her other verb, "we know not." It has often been made to prove that Mary speaks for the other women too, and so that John's narrative quietly presupposes the earlier Gospels; Ellicott allows that it may be so but will not claim more, since it may equally be that in her despair she speaks of human effort at large, hers and anyone's, as hopeless. Either way he hears it as the passionate cry of her heart over a second bereavement: they have not only crucified the Lord, they have robbed the body of the resting-place love had made for it and of the care with which love was still trying to surround it. Ellicott also marks a small lexical thing. The word for Jesus' love toward "the other disciple" here is the one used of Lazarus in John 11, not the word that stands at the cross in John 19 — Robertson notes the same imperfect of the gentler verb, and the long association of Peter and John that runs on past this chapter into Acts 3.

Gill observes that she could report the body gone only because she had already looked in, and Adam Clarke, the wesleyan-arminian, holds that she told the other apostles as well as these two, though only these two ran.

The Eastern Cyril of Jerusalem hears the Song of Songs under the scene. "By night on my bed I sought him whom my soul loved," the bride says, "I sought him, and I found him not" — and Mary came while it was yet dark, and sought the risen one, and found him not, with the tears still dropping when she ought by rights to have been dancing. Her report is therefore true in all it saw and wrong in all it concluded: the tomb is empty, and she supposes theft. Cyril lets the angels answer her out of the other Gospel, why seek ye the living among the dead, and her running carries the question to the two men who will go and look.
3:
Two men leave at once on the strength of a woman's distressed report, and the whole episode of their going belongs to this Gospel alone. Charles Ellicott, the grammatical-historical voice, marks that the details of verses 3 to 10 are peculiar to John; Luke 24 records Peter's visit only, while here the scene is pictured with the vividness and exactness of a man stating what he himself saw and took part in. He notices too a change of tense within the sentence, the second verb carrying the continuance of the journey, so that the Greek keeps them walking rather than setting them down at the grave. Robertson reads the same imperfect as a picture held open, the two having started instantly.

John Calvin, the reformed voice, finds the verse hard for a reason the others pass over. There was so little faith in the disciples and the women, he says, or rather almost none, that their great zeal is astonishing; religious feeling as such could not have sent them to seek Christ. He concludes that some seed of faith remained in their hearts, quenched for a time, so that they were not aware of having what they had — and he takes this for a pattern of how the Spirit often works in secret, a concealed root beneath visible fruit. He is scrupulous about the name: their piety was confused and mixed with much superstition, and he calls it faith only inaccurately, allowing the word because the thing was produced by the gospel alone and leaned nowhere but toward Christ. From that seed a true faith did at last spring, one that left the sepulchre behind and climbed to the heavenly glory of its object.

He presses the smallness further than mere weakness. Scripture speaks of faith's feeble beginnings as Christ being born in us and we in him; but these two must be set almost below infancy, since they do not know he is risen, and the Lord nourishes them as a mother nourishes the child still in her womb. The death of Christ had so unmade men who had once made a little progress that they needed, in Paul's phrase to the Galatians, to have Christ formed in them again, as Galatians 4 puts it. Gill notes only that Peter went forth upon hearing Mary's account.

One detail Calvin saves for the end, and it is the shrewdest thing said about the verse: Peter makes the less haste and yet is first into the tomb. Many are given more at the finish than the start promised, while others full of fervour at the outset give way when the conflict comes. The race to the grave is therefore no measure of the men, and the zeal that outran their understanding was still, on his reading, the Spirit's own work in two who could not have told you what they hoped to find.
4:
One man runs faster than another, and the witnesses divide sharply over whether that means anything. Ellicott, the grammatical-historical voice, says it does not. The outrunning is simply the result of the greater activity of John, who was probably the younger, and the pretty thought that love outran doubt or fear is not in harmony with the context, since Peter had set out just as eagerly. Robertson is content to call it a race in eagerness to reach the tomb, and Gill to say that, not content to walk, they ran, being keenly desirous to know the truth. Augustine notices only the narrator's habit: having said they came to the sepulchre, he goes back to tell us how they came, and he means himself, though he always speaks of himself as though of another man.

Matthew Henry, the puritan-evangelical voice, reads every yard of it. See what haste we should make in a good work, he says: the two consulted neither their ease nor their gravity but ran, to show the strength of their affection and lose no time — and if we are in the way of God's commandments we should run in that way. See, too, what a good thing it is to have company in a good work, for perhaps neither would have ventured to the grave alone, and being together they made no difficulty of it, as Ecclesiastes 4 says of two. And see what a laudable emulation it is among disciples to strive which shall excel in what is good: it was no breach of manners for the younger to get before the elder, and we must do our best, neither envying those who do better nor despising those who do as they can and come behind.

Then Henry does the very thing Ellicott warns against, and does it well enough to be worth reporting. The man who got foremost was the disciple whom Jesus loved in a special manner and who therefore in a special manner loved Jesus — and a sense of Christ's love to us, kindling love in us to him again, will make us excel in virtue, constraining us more than anything else to abound in duty. The man cast behind was the one who had denied his Master and was in sorrow and shame for it, and that clogged him like a weight; a sense of guilt cramps us and hinders our enlargement in God's service, and when conscience is offended we lose ground.

Two of the fathers answer a question the others never raise. Theophylact asks how the two got to the tomb at all while soldiers were guarding it, and calls it an easy question: after the rising and the earthquake and the angel's appearance the guards had withdrawn and gone to tell the Pharisees. Chrysostom notices what the evangelist does not do — he neither deprives the woman of her praise nor suppresses, out of shame, that the men had the news first from her. Gregory says only that these two came before the rest because they loved most. Between them the readings leave the verse doing double duty: a remembered detail too small for an inventor to bother with, and a race whose order the man who won it reports about himself in the third person.
5:
Why a man should have to stoop at all is answered by the architecture, and Gill and Lightfoot answer it together. The sepulchre was a cave with a floor, and John got only as far as that floor, the court where bearers set a bier down before the body went into one of the graves cut into the rock; those lay four cubits lower, so that standing inside the cave he still had to bow himself to see anything at all. Lightfoot sends the reader to the tract Bava Bathra for the arrangement of such burial-places, which he says he has quoted and explained elsewhere. The posture, in other words, is not reverence or grief but the plain geometry of a rich man's tomb.

Charles Ellicott, the grammatical-historical voice, works on the verb. It meant at first to stoop sideways, and was used of a harp-player bending over the strings; from that it came to mean stooping over a thing, peering into it, inquiring into it. The New Testament has it only four times — here, again at verse 11 when Mary does the same thing, and twice where the stooping is figurative, of the man who looks into the perfect law in James 1 and of the angels who desire to look into the gospel in 1 Peter 1. Ellicott keeps the present tense in English too, since it still describes the scene as it actually occurred, and reads the holding back at the entrance as wonder rather than calculation, perhaps not unmixed with fear, a man waiting for his friend.

Robertson adds the detail that does the evidential work. The participle is a present middle: the cloths are not found but lying, in position, and John notices the fact at once. If the body had been removed, those would have gone with it. Calvin, the reformed voice, makes the same argument as an argument: the linen might be regarded as spoils left to lead men to believe the resurrection, for it was not probable that the body had been stripped naked in order to be carried off — a thing no friend would have done, and not even an enemy.

Adam Clarke, the wesleyan-arminian, reads the refusal to enter as satisfaction rather than timidity: John was fully satisfied the body was not there. And Clarke notices what the disciple did not do. He did not gather up the linen as a relic, because he had too much religion and too much sense; the time of superstition, Clarke says drily, was not yet arrived. So the first evidence of the rising is a negative one, an absence framed by cloths that stayed where they were put, and the man who sees it first is content to look from the threshold and let the bolder man go in.
6:
The man who lost the race is the first one inside, and almost every witness stops on that reversal. Matthew Henry, the puritan-evangelical voice, puts it in a sentence worth keeping: John could out-run Peter, but Peter could out-dare John. Henry will not let either disciple off cheaply. The warmest affections, he says, are not always accompanied with the boldest resolutions, and many are swift to run religion's race who are not stout to fight her battles; yet John, outrun himself a moment later, did not turn back nor stand still but followed as fast as he could. Henry finds the two gifts almost never housed in one man, and reaches for David's elegy over Saul and Jonathan in 2 Samuel 1, swifter than eagles and stronger than lions, as the poetry of a thing seldom true in life.

The grammatical-historical readers find the same contrast already in the verbs. Robertson has an aorist for the entering and a present for the looking: Peter impulsively went on in and then beholds, and the verb of beholding is one of careful notice, not the mere glance John had given from outside. Ellicott makes the comparison explicit, this word expressing Peter's close observation while John did but see the cloths from without; Clarke takes the verb apart to the same end, to look steadily at a thing so as to discover what it is and be satisfied with viewing it.

Chrysostom, the Eastern voice, calls Peter the more fervid temper, who pursued the search and examined everything — and then turns the examination into proof. Had they carried him away, he argues, they would not have stripped him first; and the myrrh of the burial would have made the linen cling to the body, so that no thief would have been senseless enough to take such unnecessary pains. Theophylact reads the two men as two kinds of Christian, Peter practical and prompt, John contemplative and learned in divine things, the contemplative generally first in understanding and the practical first in act.

John Wesley, the wesleyan-arminian, looks ahead to what Peter saw folded and credits it to the angels who ministered to their Lord when he rose. Gregory, reading the same cloth, will make the napkin laid apart a figure of a suffering unlike ours. What Peter's entering settles, though, is nothing figurative: the inside of the tomb is in order, the wrappings are where they were laid, and the body alone is missing. A thief leaves disorder behind him. This grave has been left tidy, and the tidiness is the argument.
7:
One folded cloth, in its own place, carries more weight in this chapter than any speech. Gill begins with the word itself, which he takes to be Latin by origin and to mean the handkerchief with which sweat is wiped from the face; Nonnus, he reports, says it was common among the Syrians, and the Syriac version renders it the girdle or binding of the head, since the head and face of a dead man were bound with such a cloth. Gill then makes the observational point. Peter, by going in and looking about him and examining things more strictly and narrowly, noticed what neither man had seen from a stooping glance at the entrance.

Charles Ellicott, the grammatical-historical voice, says the same thing about the writer rather than about Peter. The cloth was not visible from without and lay in a separate place, perhaps toward the inner side of the tomb; and here, he judges, the minute knowledge and remembrance of an eye-witness reaches its climax, since the bare fact that the thing was folded neither escaped the writer's eye at the time nor faded from his memory afterwards. Robertson adds that the participle means rolled up, arranged in an orderly fashion, and draws the one-line conclusion: there was no haste. Adam Clarke, the wesleyan-arminian, turns the tidiness into an argument. Thieves would not have stopped to strip the body, wrap the cloths, and lay them by in separate places; and the providence of God, he says, ordered these very little matters so as to refute the story the guards were paid to tell in Matthew 28.

Calvin, the reformed voice, uses the separateness of the cloth against a relic. Those he calls the Papists pretend the whole body was sewn up in one linen garment, which they hold out to the people as the holy winding-sheet; and the pretence, he says, rests partly on not knowing Latin, since a cloth for wiping the face has been taken for a covering of the whole body. He passes over their boasting that they possess the one cloth in five or six different places, and fastens on what he finds intolerable: that the claim contradicts the evangelical history outright, and has had a miracle contrived to support it, the likeness of Christ's body remaining visible in the linen. Would an evangelist so careful to record lesser things, Calvin asks, have said nothing of that?

He is content with the plain view instead, and it is the best summary of the verse. Christ laid aside the tokens of death deliberately, and in laying them aside testified that he had clothed himself with a blessed and immortal life. The grave-clothes do not merely fail to prove a robbery; left as they were, they say what the angels have not yet been given to say.
8:
John goes in at last, and the Gospel records of him the one thing it does not record of Peter: that he believed. Gill reads the entering as courage borrowed — animated by Peter's example, and perhaps called in by Peter to be a second witness of the order in which things lay. Robertson puts the sequence in the particles: after Peter in time, and influenced by Peter's boldness. Then he draws the distinction the verse has been quoted for ever since. Peter saw more after he entered than John did at his first glance, but John saw into the meaning of it all better than Peter; Peter had more sight, John more insight. Robertson adds that John was the first to believe Jesus risen before seeing him, that Luke 24 leaves Peter still wondering, and that a few manuscripts, the Sinaitic Syriac among them, read a plural here and read it wrongly. He hears in the singular a quiet pride, the evangelist marking the moment he believed without sight, in contrast with the man who would later demand it.

Ellicott, also grammatical-historical, reaches the same place by character. The bold impetuosity of one disciple and the gentle reverence of the other are drawn in the man who went straight in and the man who stood gazing first; and the gentler character, he says, was also the more receptive. The verb for seeing here is neither of the two used in the preceding verses: it is not sight from a distance, nor the beholding of what lies immediately before the eye, but seeing with the mind and grasping the truth underneath the things in view. One who had believed already found in this a stepping-stone to a higher faith.

Calvin, the reformed voice, will not allow the smaller reading. To make the word mean only that John credited Mary's report of a body carried off is a poor exposition, he says, for the verb never bears that sense when it stands simply and alone; and John elsewhere uses just this phrasing for an increase of faith. That the men went home still perplexed does not contradict it. Luke's own account of Peter marvelling at the good order of the tomb means, on Calvin's reading, that even Peter was thinking of something greater and loftier than Mary had told him.

Against them stand the plainer readers. Clarke, the wesleyan-arminian, holds that John saw the body was not there and believed it had been taken away as Mary said, but did not believe him risen; Wesley says the same in a line, and Augustine had said it long before, that the disciple saw the sepulchre empty and believed the woman, since as yet they knew not the Scripture. Where a reader lands depends on how much weight the next verse is made to carry.
9:
An evangelist writing of himself in the third person here records his own dullness, and the witnesses take the admission seriously. Gill holds that the scripture meant is not one passage but the Old Testament writings at large, wherever they spoke of a rising by type or by prophecy; and he names the cause. Partly it was plain slowness, partly a settled prejudice in favour of a Messiah who would stay and set up a temporal kingdom, so that even the disciple who had leaned on his breast and the disciple who was forever asking what the Master meant had taken in neither the words nor the places they pointed to.

The grammatical-historical readers supply the texts. Robertson thinks chiefly of Psalm 16, notes that Jesus had foretold his rising repeatedly and that it was all forgotten in the great sorrow — the chief priests, by an irony he does not labour, remembered the prediction well enough in Matthew 27 — and marks the divine must that reappears in Luke 24. Barnes lists the predictions and their apostolic use, and Clarke, giving the Hebrew of the psalm, calls the ignorance of the two men a reproach. Ellicott dates the change from this moment: from here they recognised in the absent body the truth that he must rise.

Calvin, the reformed voice, reads the verse as John's self-accusation and will not let it be softened. They had often heard from Christ's own mouth what they now saw with their eyes; the failure flowed from their hearts. Warned by a strange spectacle, they begin to think of him as having something divine about him, though still far from accurate knowledge. And John deepens the charge against himself and his brethren, Calvin says, by adding not merely that they had forgotten the words but that they did not believe, since to this ignorance the whole deficiency of their faith is traced.

From that Calvin draws the lesson and then does the work. When we are ignorant of what we ought to know about Christ, the fault lies in our own carelessness with scriptures that reveal him. A reader may think the resurrection taught there only obscurely and under figures; an attentive one finds clear testimony in quantity. Calvin instances Paul at Acts 13 arguing from the sure mercies promised in Isaiah 55, which an unskilful person might think beside the point until he sees that if Christ is to secure the grace of God to us for ever, Christ himself must live for ever. Then three passages: that God will not permit his Holy One to see corruption, which Peter and Paul rightly explain of Christ, since no son of Adam is of himself exempt from it; the word to sit at the right hand until enemies are made a footstool, which requires a kingdom held to the end of the world and so a life to hold it; and Isaiah 53, where the prophet foretells the death and then at once goes further. The doctrine of scripture, Calvin ends, is full enough that whatever is defective in our faith should be charged to our ignorance of it.
10:
Two men have seen the inside of an empty tomb, and they go home. Ellicott, the grammatical-historical voice, means lodgings in Jerusalem rather than houses of their own, and reads the departure as the natural end of an errand accomplished: one of them at least had grasped, and must have said so to his friend, that the Lord was not to be looked for in the grave and that Mary's fear of enemies was groundless. They return with that truth to turn over, or to carry to the rest of the Eleven, or simply to wonder and wait until he should come as he had promised. Robertson gives the phrase its homely force, to their own place, and remembers that this disciple had taken the mother of Jesus to his home at John 19 and may well have hurried back to tell her.

Calvin, the reformed voice, is less willing to call it settled. Their minds may still have been in doubt and uncertainty on the road back; the faith was not strong but a confused remembrance of the miracle, something like a trance, until it should be more fully confirmed, since no sight of grave-clothes by itself could produce a strong faith. Christ did not present himself, Calvin adds, until they had been further awakened out of their carnal stupidity — and though their haste to the tomb was a praiseworthy demonstration of zeal, he hid himself from them because they sought him with too much superstition.

The Eastern and Latin fathers all notice who stayed. Chrysostom will not have the contrast taken as a reproach to Peter and John, who had seen the cloths, believed, and gone away astonished; it is rather that Mary's was a feeble nature which did not yet have the account of the rising accurately, and that the sight of the tomb itself comforted her. He wonders in passing why the two did not set off at once for Galilee as they had been told before the Passion, and supposes they were waiting for the others and were still at the height of their amazement. Augustine puts the same thing the other way round: while the men returned, the weaker sex was fastened to the place by a stronger affection, and eyes that had sought the Lord and not found him had nothing left to do but weep. He adds the sharper observation — her grief was deeper that he had been taken from the sepulchre than that he had been slain on the tree, as though with such a Master the withdrawal of his living presence had carried off the memory of him too.

Gregory sets Mary beside the departing men in a line that has outlived his commentary: her soul burned with love, and she did not retire from the sepulchre when the others did. Chrysostom draws the consequence that governs the rest of the chapter. She received no small reward for that zeal, and what the disciples did not see, the woman saw first.
11:
Everyone else has gone, and a woman is left looking into a hole in a rock she has already looked into. Why she should look twice is the question the witnesses answer differently, and Augustine, the Latin voice, is the one who refuses to answer it. Why she did so, he says, I know not — for she was not ignorant that the body was gone, having carried that news herself, and the two men had come and entered and not found it either. All he will offer is a guess: perhaps her grief was so excessive that she could hardly believe even her own eyes.

Matthew Henry, the puritan-evangelical voice, takes the same action as instruction. She stayed where her Master had lain because that was the likeliest place to hear tidings of him, and Henry turns the staying into a rule: where there is true love to Christ there will be a constant adherence to him, and this woman, rather than seem to desert him, will keep by his grave for his sake and go on loving him when she has lost the comfort of loving him. He reads the second look the way anyone reads a search for something mislaid — we go back again and again to the place we last had it — and says she will look yet seven times, not knowing but that she may see some encouragement at length. Weeping, he insists, must not hinder seeking; and those are likeliest to seek and find who seek with affection and seek in tears.

Henry even itemises the tears, and the list is better than a summary of it. She wept at the remembrance of his bitter sufferings; she wept for his death and for what she and her friends and the whole country had lost by it; she wept to think of going home without him; she wept because she could not now so much as find his body. Those who seek Christ, he adds, must seek him sorrowing, and must weep not for him but for themselves — and he sends the reader to Hosea 6, where the third day brings a raising up to those who follow on to know.

The grammatical-historical readers keep the picture exact. Robertson hears a past perfect for her standing and an imperfect for her weeping, a woman left weeping by a tomb, which he calls a pathetic and common enough sight. Ellicott traces her movements: she had gone back to tell the disciples, followed them out again, and now that they have returned is alone at the place. Clarke notes only that she remained some while after the two had gone. Calvin, the reformed voice, marks that the evangelist is now beginning to describe how Christ appeared, and thinks it probable that the other women were with her even though one alone is named. Henry notes what Mark says plainly, that the risen Christ appeared first to Mary Magdalene in Mark 16 — so the last person at the grave is the first person to the Lord.
12:
Two figures in white, seated at either end of an empty ledge, and the first thing most of the witnesses reach for is the furniture of the tabernacle. Lightfoot sets them where the cherubim stood at each end of the mercy-seat in Exodus 25, and then wanders, profitably, into what the rabbis made of the cherubim of Solomon's temple in 2 Chronicles 3. Onkelos the proselyte, he reports from Bava Bathra, said the cherubim are like children going from their master, faces turned partly toward him and partly toward the road they must take; and the Gemarists held that when Israel obeyed the will of God the cherubim looked toward one another, but when Israel did not, they turned their faces to the walls. Lightfoot doubts whether Onkelos was really commenting on Chronicles, since the Targum he has to hand renders the verse of lily work instead.

Ellicott, the grammatical-historical voice, faces the evidential awkwardness squarely. This is a vision to Mary alone, recorded so fully that she must have told it to the evangelist herself, and resting therefore on her testimony; as a vision to one person it may seem less certainly objective than the appearances with several witnesses. He asks for caution in judging what lies outside the ordinary canons of evidence, and argues that if the earlier angelic vision is admitted there is no ground for rejecting this one — and that the evangelist, who had seen nothing of the kind himself, was guided to accept and record it, which Ellicott weighs as a judgment of higher authority than criticism can reach. The white, he adds, is an ellipsis for raiment, common in classical writers and in all writers; and the posture is that of sitting and watching the body. She had feared an outrage done to it, and God had given his angels charge concerning him.

Robertson notes that the two men had seen nothing, mentions Westcott's suggestion of an economy in such manifestations, and prefers to own our ignorance of why only the women saw them; he gathers the parallel garments from Mark 16 and Luke 24, and reads the last verb as an imperfect of what had been lying there and was not there now. Gill notes the Jewish expectation that good angels come in white.

Calvin, the reformed voice, is struck by the forbearance of it — so many faults borne with in Mary and her companions, and so great an honour done them, angels sent and then the Lord himself made known to them before ever he was made known to the apostles. He thinks the apostles' dullness the less excusable of the two, having had better instruction, and takes one of Christ's purposes in choosing the women to have been to shame them. White he reads as the emblem of heavenly glory, as at the transfiguration in Matthew 17 and with the angel who stood before Cornelius in Acts 10: linen was ordinary enough in the East, but God marked these out as something uncommon. Whether their bodies were real he declines to settle, calling it a useless inquiry. That Matthew names one angel he does not find contradictory, since both did not speak at once but only the one commissioned to. And he lets go of Augustine's allegory of a gospel preached from east to west for something he thinks worthier of notice: by the honour the angels pay this grave, the ignominy of the cross is taken away and the heavenly majesty of Christ begins to shine.
13:
Angels ask her a question and she answers it as though two strangers had wandered into a graveyard. Gill makes that the point: she spoke without any concern about what they were, as if they had been of the human kind, because her grief had made her fearless and she cared not to whom she opened her case if only she could get some tidings. He notes that Beza's ancient copy, and the Ethiopic version with it, add a second question here, whom seekest thou. Ellicott, the grammatical-historical voice, hears the difference between this answer and her earlier one: there she said we know not, here she says I know not, and being alone with strangers she may have used the singular whether or not she had come out with other women. The feeling of the earlier verse still has entire possession of her, he says, and is now the more fervent for being spoken to men she does not know.

Barnes and Clarke account for what she assumes. It was conjectured from the burial notice in John 19 that the body had been laid in this tomb only for the Sabbath, to be carried afterwards to a fitter place; Mary seems to be reckoning with exactly that, and to suppose that friends of his have come early and got there before her. Calvin, the reformed voice, infers from the other evangelists that the angel held a long conversation and that John gives only a brief summary of it, enough to prove the resurrection and no more. The exchange, as he reads it, is reproof mingled with comfort: she is reproved for excessive grief and told in the same breath that there is no reason to weep, since Christ has risen.

Matthew Henry, the puritan-evangelical voice, takes the question apart. It is a rebuke to her weeping — why weep, when you have cause to rejoice? — and Henry observes that many of the floods of our tears would dry away before such a search into the fountain of them. It shows, second, how much angels are concerned at the griefs of the saints, having a charge to minister to them for their comfort, which he thinks Christians should copy toward each other. And it is asked, third, only to make an occasion of telling her the thing that would turn her mourning into rejoicing, put off her sackcloth and gird her with gladness.

Her answer, in Henry's reading, shows two things at once. It shows the weakness of her faith, since faith as a grain of mustard seed would have removed this mountain; and he generalises it, that we perplex ourselves with imaginary difficulties which faith would show us to be real advantages, and that many good people complain of clouds and darkness which are the necessary methods of grace for humbling the soul and endearing Christ to it. It shows also the strength of her love. She is not diverted from her inquiry by the surprise of the vision, nor satisfied with the honour of having been granted it, but harps still on the one string. Gill reads the angels' question the same way — she had no reason to weep but to rejoice, since he was risen and alive.
14:
She turns round for no stated reason and finds the man she is looking for standing in front of her, and does not know him. Ellicott, the grammatical-historical voice, declines to invent a cause for the turn, and says that if there was one it is useless to ask what. She has spoken her woe and turns aside again to weep, and in turning sees another figure. Weighed down by sorrow, not looking intently, perhaps seeing indistinctly through tear-filled eyes, she fails to recognise her Lord — and Ellicott is candid that nobody knows what there was to recognise. Figure, feature and clothing there must have been, but differing in this manifestation, as in others, from what they had been used to. She may hardly have looked at all, assuming that the only person about a garden at that hour would be the man who kept it. Robertson reads her turning as instinct, a woman feeling someone behind her.

Clarke, the wesleyan-arminian, understands the movement as the beginning of a departure: she was turning back to follow the other women to Jerusalem, who had already gone, though she was not yet out of the garden. He notes too what John leaves out — the angels' announcement that he was risen, omitted, Clarke supposes, because the other three had told it so particularly. And he makes the recognition failure a matter of unpreparedness rather than of eyesight. She was so absorbed in grief that she gave his person little attention, and she could not have imagined such an appearance possible, having no conception of a rising from the dead; she was, he says, every way unprepared to know him.

Calvin, the reformed voice, asks the question directly: whence the mistake, in a woman who must have known him intimately? Some answer that he appeared in a different form. Calvin puts the fault in the eyes of the women instead, as Luke 24 says of the two on the road, whose eyes were holden. He will not have Christ continually assuming new shapes, as though he were the shifting sea-god of the fables, whom Calvin names in Greek and whose legend the edition's own note follows out at length through Herodotus and Ovid; for it is in the power of God, who gave men eyes, to lessen the sharpness of their vision whenever he thinks proper.

Barnes agrees on the ordinary grounds, that she was not expecting to see him and that it was still twilight and she could not see distinctly. But Calvin presses the thing further than circumstance, and the application is the sharpest sentence written on the verse. In Mary we have an example of the mistakes the human mind falls into habitually: Christ presents himself to our view, and we imagine he is taking some other shape, so that our senses conceive of anything sooner than the true Christ. Our understanding is not merely liable to be deceived, Calvin says; it is bewitched by the world and by Satan, so that it has no perception of the truth standing in front of it.
15:
A woman asks a stranger to tell her where a corpse has been put so that she can carry it off herself, and the witnesses are unanimous that the offer is absurd and that the absurdity is the point. Clarke, the wesleyan-arminian, does the arithmetic. Jesus was in the prime of life when he was crucified, and a hundred pounds weight of spices had been added to his body; yet Mary thinks of nothing less than carrying him away if only she can find where he lies. How true the proverb, Clarke says: love feels no load. He also unpacks the word she misapplies — the overseer of the garden, compounded of the word for garden and the word for inspector, the man who had charge of the workmen and the produce and rendered account to the owner.

Ellicott, the grammatical-historical voice, weighs her terms of address. The word rendered Sir is generally respectful but, like its equivalent in most languages, was used to a stranger and even to an inferior; and what the English calls a gardener answered more nearly to a bailiff, a servant of the man who owned the tomb, who might for that reason have become known to her at the embalming. Her verb repays attention too: it means to bear, then to bear away or remove, and then to remove secretly, a sense with many undoubted examples in Josephus and the one used of Judas and the bag in John 12. So she is not accusing him of tidying the garden but of spiriting the body off.

Ellicott notices one more thing, and it is the most human detail in the verse. Three times she speaks of the Lord by a bare pronoun. She had named him a moment earlier and may suppose the man overheard; but the impression her eagerness leaves is of a mind so wholly filled with one subject that it assumes every other mind is filled with it too. Devotion of that kind does not weigh difficulties. A place of safety for that sacred body is what her will is fixed on, and the will neither fears the danger nor notices that the thing is physically impossible, but simply asserts that she will take him away. Robertson reads the grammar the same way, with the emphasis falling on thou and then on I, and calls the whole thought a new idea as mistaken as the one before it.

Calvin, the reformed voice, grants that the title she uses was ordinary enough among her people for labourers and men of low condition, and then says the hard thing. Mary has no view of the matter but an earthly one. All she wants is to get the dead body back and keep it hidden in a tomb, and she leaves out the one thing that matters, the lifting of her mind to the divine power of his rising. We need not wonder, he concludes, if views so grovelling put a veil before her eyes. The risen Christ, meanwhile, has repeated the angels' question and added one of his own, and is standing there being mistaken for a hired man.
16:
Everything in the chapter turns on one word, and it is her own name. Gill supposes he altered the tone of his voice and called her by name in his usual manner, and draws from it the thing the verse is most used for: Christ has personal knowledge of all his people and can call them by name, knowing them and making himself known before they can know him, and though he may absent himself a while, not always. Clarke, the wesleyan-arminian, hears the uncommon emphasis and the familiar sound together, enough to prove at once who it must be, and leaves the transports of joy to be imagined. He adds the judgment the chapter bears out: she had sought him more fervently and stayed more attached than any of the others, and so to her first he shows himself, and she is made the first herald of a risen Saviour.

Barnes, grammatical-historical, takes her reply apart. The title came in three grades — the bare word for master, lowest in honour; then my master; then the form she uses, my great master, the most honourable of the three, which among the Jews had been given to only seven men, all of great eminence. As she uses it, Barnes says, it is at once an expression of joy and an acknowledgment of lordship, and he thinks she was on the point of casting herself at his feet. Ellicott notes that the better reading has the evangelist say she spoke in Hebrew, and that the word occurs nowhere else in the New Testament except on the lips of the blind man at Mark 10. Clarke records a textual curiosity in the same place: one manuscript, the later Syriac and three copies of the Old Latin add, after her exclamation, that she ran to cling to him — which supplies exactly the action the Lord's next words answer.

Ellicott reads the whole encounter as fitted to her rather than to the apostles. He who knew her whole past, and knew that her devotion had grown out of the deliverance he had worked in her, stands by this woman weeping at a grave while Peter and John have gone home; and Ellicott generalises it in two sentences worth keeping. The voice of God is always most quickly heard by the hearts that love him, and his presence is never so truly felt as in the utter helplessness of human woe.

Calvin, the reformed voice, treats the exchange as a picture of conversion. The earlier words had sounded like a stranger's; now he assumes the character of the Master and addresses his disciple by name, as the good shepherd in John 10 calls every sheep of his flock. That word enters her heart, opens her eyes, rouses all her senses, and she surrenders on the spot. Here, says Calvin, is a lively image of our calling: we are admitted to the true knowledge of Christ only when he first knows us and then familiarly invites us, not by the voice that sounds indiscriminately in every ear but by the one that calls the sheep the Father gave him — as Paul corrects himself in Galatians 4, after you have known God, or rather after you have been known by him. Her answer, he adds, is not merely respectful but a profession of obedience, a declaration that she is his disciple; such a change on a mind lately blind is the secret and wonderful work of the Spirit; and her promptness is the example, since all whom Christ invites should answer without delay.
17:
Two difficulties sit in this verse. The first is why a woman is forbidden what Thomas will later be invited to do, and the witnesses solve it from the grammar before they solve it from theology. Robertson and Ellicott agree that the verb means to cling, fasten on, grasp; the tense is present, so what is forbidden is not an act but the continuance of one. Do not go on clinging to me. Ellicott supposes she had already cast herself at his feet with the customary embrace of the knees, perhaps to make sure the body was his. Wesley renders it, detain me not now, since she will have other opportunities. Barnes marks the difference in the two cases: Thomas was told to touch because he doubted, and Mary did not doubt at all, but, full of joy, was about to prostrate herself and stay. The not yet ascended, on his reading, means not that the ascension is this instant but that it is not immediate — there is time still, and this is not the hour to spend it kneeling.

Calvin, the reformed voice, meets the apparent clash with Matthew 28, where the women hold him by the feet and are not rebuked. His answer is that they were not repelled until their eagerness had been carried to excess: so far as touch was needed to remove doubt he did not forbid it, but seeing their whole attention taken up with embracing him he restrained an immoderate zeal fixed on a bodily presence and understanding nothing beyond it. Ellicott makes the same point from the other end, that her act assumed a state of things not yet brought about — he had not come back to stay among them in the presence of the Paraclete, whose coming depended on his going, and she had not yet learned the hardest sentence in the farewell discourse, that it is expedient for them that he go away, in John 16.

The second difficulty is the careful doubling of the names, and here Wesley is the sharpest. He does not say Our God, Wesley observes, for no creature can be raised to an equality with him; the Father is his in a singular and incommunicable manner, and ours through him in such a kind as a creature is capable of. Ellicott reads the phrase as more emphatic than our Father would have been, and spells out the logic: because he is my Father he is also yours, and you are my brethren; the victory over death was man's victory, in whose nature death was conquered, and the ascension will be that nature's ascension. The word brethren itself, he notes, declares the continuance of his humanity, as Hebrews 2 has it. Gill keeps the distinction plain — his Father by nature, theirs by grace and adoption.

Wesley hears in that one word the forgiveness of their desertion intimated in the strongest way without ever being mentioned, and calls these exquisite touches, everywhere abundant in the evangelical writings, proof of how perfectly Christ knew our frame. Calvin dismisses the reading that confines brethren to Christ's kinsmen on the strength of John 7, since Mary in fact went to the disciples, which settles whom he meant. He will not let the departure be heard as a loss either: Christ ascends to be present with his own by divine power, absent in body yet reigning at the right hand over heaven and earth, which is why those risen with him are told to seek the things above in Colossians 3. Barnes adds its pastoral weight: nothing was better fitted to console them than the assurance that his God was theirs, and that though he had been slain they were bound indissolubly to the same Father.
18:
The errand is discharged in one sentence, and Matthew Henry, the puritan-evangelical voice, notices whom she has to find in order to discharge it. Peter and John had left her seeking him carefully with tears and would not stay to seek with her; she now comes to the whole company, gathered together, to tell them she has found him. Henry makes much of the correction involved. She had set them off after a dead body and must now put right the mistake she led them into, for what she found was a living body and a glorified one — so that she got what she sought and something infinitely better. She had joy in the sight of the Master and was willing to share it, knowing it would be good news to them; and Henry turns that into the rule, that when God comforts us it is with the design that we may comfort others.

He notices too that she carried both halves of the commission. She told them what she had seen and also what she had heard, which was itself a good token: he had spoken these things to her as a message to be delivered, and she delivered it faithfully. Those acquainted with the word of Christ, Henry adds, should pass their knowledge on for the good of others and not grudge that others should know as much as they do. Elsewhere in the same comment he draws the line that governs the whole scene: a sight of angels and their smiles will not suffice without a sight of Jesus. And he observes that Christ, in making himself known to those who seek him, often outdoes their expectations, and that his way of doing it is by his word applied to the soul, spoken to that person in particular.

The grammatical-historical readers keep the order of her words exact. Robertson notes that she announces the fact before she delivers the message, and that the perfect tense of "I have seen the Lord" means she will carry that sight in her heart for good. Ellicott observes that the coming is described from the standpoint of the writer, who was one of the disciples she came to. Gill reads her promptness as cheerfulness, a woman glad to go on such an errand, whatever her own love might have preferred.

Clarke, the wesleyan-arminian, supplies what John leaves unsaid and what makes the verse more than a happy ending. According to Mark 16 they could not believe what she said, and treated it as an effect of her troubled imagination. The first preacher of the resurrection was heard out and disbelieved — which is, on any accounting, a strange thing for the church to have remembered about itself, and a stronger argument than any the chapter makes on purpose.
19:
A detail that looks like scene-setting is the one the witnesses fight over: the doors were shut. Ellicott, the grammatical-historical voice, holds that John notes it here and again at verse 26 to mark the appearance as preternatural. The risen body was the body of his human life, not subject to that life's ordinary conditions; the power that upheld it on the water in John 6 made it through those forty days independent of gravitation and material resistance. He rejects the alternative that the doors were opened miraculously, as for Peter in Acts 12, since the context gives no such impression and so striking an incident would have been mentioned.

Barnes and Clarke take the other road. Barnes points out that the words mean closed, not fastened, and finds no evidence of a miraculous entry at all — for anything in the text Jesus came in the usual way, and it was the suddenness that alarmed them. Clarke agrees and states the principle flatly: where there is no need for a miracle, a miracle is never wrought. He adds that the Jews are nowhere said to have designed anything against the disciples, Christ's word in John 18 having let them go; weak faith made them expect to be next. Augustine, the Latin voice, cuts across the argument. Some are indisposed to believe the miracle and ask how a body that hung on the cross could pass a shut door; but comprehend the manner of it, he answers, and it is no miracle, for when reason fails faith is edified. The shut door did not hinder a body in which divinity resided, and he who entered without open doors was born without violation of his mother's virginity. Theophylact reads the closed doors as sign, showing he had risen the same way, with the stone still lying on the tomb.

On why they were shut the readings converge. Bede finds the infirmity of the apostles written in it: they met behind doors through the same fear that had scattered them before, and the Lord came at evening because that is when they would be most afraid. Theophylact suggests instead that he waited until all were gathered. Ellicott fills in its grounds — the Shepherd struck and the flock scattered, his warnings of persecution in John 15 fresh in mind, and charges possible against particular men, since Peter had drawn the high priest's household on himself. Calvin, the reformed voice, adds that all were assembled in one place not without God's providence, so that the event might be the more certain. Barnes notes what the gathering became: the first assembly convened for worship on the Lord's day, and one in which Jesus was present.

Chrysostom, the Eastern voice, explains the timing by what Mary's news had done to them. They were left obliged either to disbelieve her or, believing, to grieve that he had not counted them worthy of the sight; and he would not let them pass a whole day so, but came while their desire was still trembling. It is wonderful, he adds, that they did not take him for a phantom — but Mary had guarded against that by the faith she had worked in them, and he showed himself openly and steadied them with his voice. The greeting means simply, be not disturbed, and recalls what he had said before the crucifixion, that his peace he gave them and that in him they should have peace. Ellicott hears more than reassurance. The familiar words came to them as her own name had come to Mary, but they are also a voice out of the darkness beyond the grave into which the living have tried in vain to see — and that voice is one of peace, the conqueror's word that the victory is won, and a message of atonement carried through them to all mankind.
20:
He proves who he is by showing them the places where he was killed. Robertson, grammatical-historical, states the dogmatic weight of it without apology: this body, not yet glorified, retained the marks of the nails and of the soldier's spear, which he calls ample proof of a bodily resurrection both against the modern view that only Christ's spirit arose and against the Docetic notion that he never had an actual human body. Clarke, the wesleyan-arminian, says the same more quietly — the marks were preserved so that the disciples might be the more fully convinced that the rising was real. Gill reads the gesture as kindness before it is evidence: having greeted them in the most tender manner, he acted to put them out of all pain and let them know with certainty who he was.

Barnes raises the question the wounds invite and answers it from necessity. That body had not yet put on its glorified form, and could not have: the proof of the resurrection had to be established first, and it could be established only by his appearing as he was when he died. Augustine, the Latin voice, answers it the other way, and the two readings are worth setting side by side. The glory with which the righteous shall shine like the sun in their Father's kingdom was, he holds, present in Christ's body and merely veiled — not absent — and he accommodated his presence to the weak sight of men, presenting himself in a form his disciples could look at and recognise. Gregory adds the plain reason for the gesture: their faith wavered even with the material body standing before them, and so he showed them hands and side. Augustine notes which wound came from which instrument, the nails in the hands and the lance in the side, and says the marks were kept for the healing of doubting hearts.

Calvin, the reformed voice, takes up the objection that scars are beneath the glory of a risen Lord. Let the objector consider, first, that Christ rose not so much for himself as for us, and second, that whatever contributes to our salvation is glorious to Christ: his humbling himself for a time took nothing from his majesty, and marks that serve to confirm belief in his rising do not diminish his glory either. But Calvin will not have the inference run the other way. To conclude from this that Christ still bears a pierced side would be absurd; the use of the marks was temporary, until the apostles were fully convinced, and what the whole scene accomplishes is that all the grief occasioned them by his death was dispelled by his new life.

On the gladness itself the witnesses are precise, and none of them makes it simple. Ellicott notes that Luke gives hands and feet where John gives hands and side, the pierced side being John's own detail, and traces the emotion's course: their first impression had been that they saw a spirit and they were afraid, and it was the conviction of corporeal identity, given in the wounds, that turned fear into joy. Robertson adds from Luke 24 that they disbelieved for joy, it being too good to be true, terror having seized them first because of the suddenness of the appearing and the state they were already in. Chrysostom lets the promise answer itself: what he had said before the crucifixion, that he would see them again and their heart should rejoice, is now fulfilled — and Robertson points to the same word at John 16.
21:
The greeting is given a second time, and Ellicott, the grammatical-historical voice, thinks the repetition is not a repetition at all. The first words were greeting; these, he judges, are farewell, other words having intervened as Luke shows. He is about to withdraw the evidence of his presence, and does so with the customary peace — but in the same breath reminds them of the apostleship he has called them to, gives an earnest of a presence that will never leave them, and sets the greatness of the work before them.

On the sending itself Ellicott is at his fullest. The words identify them with Christ in his mediatorial work: he is the great Apostle of Hebrews 3, and they are ambassadors to whom he commits the ministry of reconciliation in 2 Corinthians 5. He stands to the Father as they now stand to him. What he declared, they are in his name to declare — the fulness of the Father's love and the peace between man and God, witnessed in his life and death. And they stand to the world as he stood to it. At this very moment, Ellicott notes, they are behind shut doors for fear of men who are triumphing over him as dead; and it is to that world, which will hate and persecute and kill them as it hated and killed him, that they are sent, with forgiveness and mercy and peace to declare to every heart that does not harden against them, finding in his presence the support he had always found in the Father's.

Calvin, the reformed voice, reads the verse as an ordination and dates the apostolic office from it. They had been sent through Judea before, but only as heralds commanding that the supreme Teacher be heard, not as apostles charged with a perpetual office of teaching; now the Lord ordains them his ambassadors to establish his kingdom in the world, and Calvin would have it held as settled that the apostles were at this moment first appointed ordinary ministers of the gospel. The words declare, he says, that Christ has discharged a teacher's office, finished his course, and now confers it on them — the Father having appointed him to point out the way for a time and then put others in his room to supply his absence, which is why Ephesians 4 speaks of a ministry given to govern the church to the end. The preaching is therefore perpetual, not brief.

He is careful about the limit of the transfer. Their ministry needed ratifying so, he grants, since they were unknown men of mean condition; Christ therefore communicates his own authority, declaring that the gospel came to them not by human warrant but by God's command. Yet he does not substitute them in his room so as to resign the highest teaching authority, which the Father vested in him alone. He continues, and will eternally continue, the only Teacher of the church; the one difference is that he spoke with his own mouth while he dwelt on earth and now speaks by the apostles.

The remaining readers keep to the pattern of the sending. Barnes paraphrases it as it must have sounded: as God sent me to preach, to be persecuted and to suffer, so I send you — Christ being their model. Clarke has them clothed with the very same authority and influenced by the very same Spirit. Robertson notes that both Greek verbs of sending appear here in practically the same sense, and that the perfect tense leaves Christ still bearing the Father's commission as he hands on theirs. Wesley makes the most practical observation of the four: peace in a man's own soul is the foundation of a true gospel minister's mission, as 2 Corinthians 4 implies; Christ was the apostle of the Father, and Peter and the rest the apostles of Christ.
22:
He breathes on them, and the word John chooses for it is the one the Greek Old Testament uses when God breathes into the nostrils of the first man. Ellicott, the grammatical-historical voice, notes that the verb occurs nowhere else in the New Testament and was familiar from Genesis 2, and reads the choice as deliberate memory: the evangelist writes as one who recalled that the influence of that moment on their later lives was a new spiritual creation, by which they were called out of death into life. It was the first step, he says, in the great moral change that passed over the disciples after the crucifixion and reached its completion at Pentecost. Robertson identifies the same Septuagint word and adds Ezekiel 37, where breath is commanded into the slain.

Barnes sets the gesture among the prophetic sign-acts, the significant deeds the prophets used to represent a message, as at the potter's house in Jeremiah 18. Here the breathing represents both the nature of the coming influence and its source, the word for spirit meaning wind and air and breath as well, which is why the Spirit's operations are compared to wind in John 3. Clarke, the wesleyan-arminian, takes the creation allusion further: they were to be made new men to be fit for the work, and as Adam was before God breathed the quickening spirit into him, so is every soul until it receives this breathing. Nothing of God, Clarke insists, is seen or known or felt but through it, and no man ever preached so as to convert without it. From this verse, he notes, the Spirit's influences came to be called inspiration at all, the word being simply a breathing into.

The hard question is what exactly was given, and Ellicott faces it squarely. The words are not merely a promise of a future gift, since they are a definite imperative about the moment in which they were spoken; neither are they the promised coming of the Paraclete, since that gift was not yet, because Jesus was not yet glorified, as John 7 says. What he gave was a sign which to faithful hearts was itself the firstfruits of what was coming — an act Ellicott calls sacramental, with inward grace attending the outward token. He notices that the word of giving is the same that stood at Take, eat, this is my body, in Matthew 26, and that the command itself implies the power to obey. Wesley puts the same thought in a sentence: as they receive this breath out of his mouth, so they receive the Spirit out of his fulness, and this was an earnest of Pentecost. Barnes calls the breathing a certain sign or pledge of what would come upon them.

Calvin, the reformed voice, reads the act as equipment for an impossible office. To govern the church of God, to carry the embassy of eternal salvation, to erect God's kingdom on earth and raise men to heaven is a task far beyond human capacity, and no man is found qualified unless the Spirit inspire him, since by 1 Corinthians 12 no one can even speak a word concerning Christ unless the Spirit guide his tongue. It is Christ's own glory, he adds, to form those he appoints as teachers, the fulness of the Spirit having been poured on him so that he might bestow it on each by measure; and the symbol here would not apply at all if the Spirit did not proceed from him. From that Calvin turns on the bishops who, in ordaining priests, boast of breathing the Holy Spirit on them, and says the difference between that and this is plain enough to the senses. Cyril of Jerusalem, the Eastern voice, states the fact without the argument: the fellowship of this Holy Spirit he bestowed upon the apostles.
23:
Lightfoot asks the question that organises the verse: is this the authority Christ had already given them, or more? He argues for more, on two grounds. It would be incongruous for the Saviour to use an action so new and unwonted as breathing on them merely to vest them with a power already conferred; and the earlier binding and loosing concerned only the articles and decisions of the law, whereas this reaches the sins of mankind — that power concerned doctrines, this one the persons of men. He sets beside it the commission in Luke 24, that repentance and remission of sins be preached in his name among all nations, and supposes those words came first.

Robertson and Barnes read it the other way, as the rabbinical metaphor of binding and loosing by proclaiming and teaching that stands at Matthew 16 and Matthew 18. Robertson is blunt about the limit: the power to forgive sin belongs only to God, and Jesus claimed it for himself; what he commits to the disciples is the privilege of giving assurance of God's forgiveness by correctly announcing its terms. There is no proof, he says, that he transferred to them or to anyone after them the power in themselves to forgive, and he takes the keys to be put into the hands of all believers who will tell the story of Christ's love.

Barnes presses a related point about who received it. Jesus confers the same power on all the apostles and gives none any peculiar authority; had one been appointed to pre-eminence, Barnes finds it remarkable that the Saviour does not hint at it here. The meaning, on his reading, is not that a man can forgive sins at all, but that these men were inspired — taught by the Spirit to declare on what terms and to what temper of mind God extends forgiveness, establishing in the churches the conditions on which men may be pardoned, with the promise that God would confirm what they taught. That, he says, is as far as possible from a claimed authority to pronounce pardon.

Ellicott, the grammatical-historical voice, grounds the authority in the two preceding verses — their being sent as Christ was sent, and their reception of the Spirit, by whom Christ is himself present in them — and then states the asymmetry that makes the saying bearable. God has promised forgiveness wherever there is repentance; he has not promised repentance wherever there is sin. From every declaration of forgiveness made in the Father's name it follows both that hearts which penitently accept it receive remission, and that the hardness of hearts which wilfully reject it is increased by the rejecting, so that the very words by which their sins would have been remitted become the words by which they are retained. He adds a fine observation on the tenses: in the better text the first verb is a strict present and the second a perfect-present, hard to keep in English, but the thought is that where sins are remitted a change of condition is taking place, and where they are retained the condition remains what it was.

The remaining voices guard the same boundary. Gill insists that God only can forgive sins, that the apostles never assumed any such power, and that to claim it is the mark of antichrist, their work being to declare the terms of reconciliation. Calvin, the reformed voice, holds that this power must not be separated from the office of teaching, since it is the preaching of the gospel that remits or retains. Wesley reduces it to a conditional: supposing them to repent and believe, their sins are remitted; supposing them to remain impenitent, they are retained. And Cyril of Jerusalem, the Eastern voice, ties the authority back to the gift just given, the fellowship of the Holy Spirit bestowed on the apostles.
24:
A single man's absence is recorded, and the witnesses treat it as the hinge of everything that follows. Lightfoot takes the double name first, and insists the evangelist is not doing a lexicographer's work here. He is not translating a Hebrew word into Greek but telling us the man was called Thomas among the Hebrews and Didymus among the Greeks — said of no one else among the twelve, since Simon called Peter and Nathanael called Bartholomew carry two distinct names apiece, while these are one name of one meaning in two tongues. Lightfoot guesses he was born where Jews and Greeks lived intermingled, and offers the region of Decapolis. Robertson adds that the group is still called the twelve though Judas is dead.

Why he was away is answered from the state of the company. Lightfoot recalls that all had fled when Christ was seized, as Mark 14 says, except the two; which is why Mary went to Peter and the other disciple at the start of the chapter, knowing where those two were and not the rest. Scattered so, they passed the sabbath, and only on hearing their Lord was risen began to associate again. Chrysostom reaches the same conclusion from the other end: probably, after the recent dispersion, this man had simply not come back yet.

On the character of his refusal, Chrysostom and Clarke are severe in different registers. Chrysostom opens with a balance — to believe carelessly and at random comes of an over-easy temper, but to be curious and meddlesome beyond measure marks a gross understanding — and holds Thomas blameworthy on the second count. He did not disbelieve the apostles so much as judge the thing impossible, which is why he said not that he disbelieved them but that he would not believe till he had put his hand in; and he asked proof from the grossest of the senses, not trusting even his eyes, lest what he saw prove an apparition. Clarke traces the hardening in three stages. The unbelief was unreasonable, since ten brethren testified and he rejected their testimony; then obstinate, since he was determined to believe on no evidence God might choose to give but only on his own terms; then presumptuous, since a sight of the person would not do unless he could get his finger into the nail-holes and his hand into the spear-wound.

Clarke turns it into the plainest warning in the chapter. By absenting himself he lost this opportunity of seeing and hearing Christ and of receiving at that hour the inestimable blessing of the Spirit, when he ought to have remembered that where two or three are assembled in Christ's name he is among them, as Matthew 18 promised. He had lost much good and gained much evil and was insensible of it. Jesus comes to the meeting, Clarke says, and a disciple is found out of a place he might have been in, and is not only unblessed but hardened; it was God's mere mercy that he ever had another opportunity.

Chrysostom will not end there, and the turn he makes is the one the next verses justify. Seeing the unbelief of the disciple, he says, consider the lovingkindness of the Lord, who for the sake of a single soul showed himself with his wounds and came to save even one, though that one was grosser than the rest. Calvin, the reformed voice, puts the same providence more coolly: the unbelief of Thomas is related so that by means of it the faith of the godly may be the more fully confirmed — though he grants the man was not merely slow and reluctant but obstinate. Ellicott finds the absence in character, true to the desponding temper that had earlier reckoned a journey to Jerusalem a journey to death in John 11.
25:
The witnesses split over this man more sharply than over anything else in the chapter, and the division is worth stating before the detail. Calvin, the reformed voice, finds in the demand the root of a general vice, that everyone wishes to be wise out of his own understanding and flatters himself beyond measure. The words have no approach to faith, he says, but are what he calls a sensual judgment — one founded on the perception of the senses — and the same thing happens to all who are so devoted to their own sense that they leave no room for the word of God. Barnes takes almost the opposite view. It is not known, he says, what the ground of the incredulity was; probably it was in part the effect of deep grief and of the despondency that fills the mind when a long-cherished hope is taken away, and in such a case it takes proof of uncommon clearness to convince a man he may yet have what he wants. Thomas has been much blamed by expositors, Barnes adds, but he asked only for proof that would be satisfactory in his circumstances.

Barnes then puts the episode to a use none of the others attempts. The incident shows, as the whole conduct of the apostles shows, that they had not conspired together to impose on the world: even they were slow to believe, and one of them refused to rely on the testimony of ten of his brethren. How unlike this, he asks, is the conduct of men who agree to foist a story on mankind. And he turns it on the reader — many now are unwilling to believe because they do not see, with just as little reason as this man had, when the testimony of eleven men who saw him alive after the crucifixion, who were willing to die attesting it, and who had nothing whatever to gain by imposture, should be reckoned ample proof.

Ellicott, the grammatical-historical voice, weighs the wording. He hears in the refusal to admit the testimony of eyewitnesses, and those the whole of his ten brethren, an echo of the question this same disciple had once put to Christ himself about not knowing the way. He notes a textual variant in the second clause, where the Greek for print and the Greek for place differ by a single letter and copyists might easily take one for the other: read as place it answers to the touch of the finger, as print answers to the sight of the eye, though the repetition either way expresses a determination almost amounting to obstinacy. Calvin reports the same variant and declines to decide, telling the reader to choose. Ellicott observes that the feet go unmentioned, since hands and side would be demonstrative evidence by themselves, and warns against inferring from the silence that the feet were not nailed. The refusal itself, he notes, stands in the strongest form the language allows, a double negative: I will by no means believe.

Two smaller observations frame it. Robertson notices that the brethren report the thing in the very words Mary had used, and that the reply comes back as a triple negative condition. Lightfoot recalls a rabbinic tradition in which Moses was charged with just this weakness — told that the people had corrupted themselves, he took the tables and would not believe Israel had sinned, saying that if he did not see he would not believe — and the retort that follows it, whether he would not have believed without seeing. The demand, in other words, was an old failing with a pedigree, and it is about to be met rather than scolded.
26:
A week passes before he comes again, and Matthew Henry, the puritan-evangelical voice, asks why the delay and gives two answers. The first is about the nature of the risen life: he deferred the next appearance to show the disciples he was not risen to the life he had formerly lived among them, conversing with them constantly, but was now one belonging to another world and visiting this one as angels do, now and then, as there was occasion. Where he was in the interval, Henry says bluntly, it is folly to inquire and presumption to determine; and he sets the forty days of his glory, for the most part unseen and attended by good spirits, beside the forty days at the beginning of his ministry when he was unseen and tempted by the evil one in Matthew 4.

The second answer is a rebuke. The man who had missed the former meeting could not have another such opportunity for several days, and Henry draws the proverb out of it: he that slips one tide must stay a good while for another. A melancholy week, he reckons, the absent disciple had of it. Clarke, the wesleyan-arminian, reads the same week from the other side — it was precisely that day se'nnight, the apostles' weekly meeting, and though the man had not been found at the former one he was determined not to be absent from this. According to his custom, Clarke adds, Jesus came again, for he cannot forget his promise where two or three are assembled in his name.

That weekly pattern is itself disputed. Barnes takes the appearance as evidence that the apostles had thus early set this day apart, and reasons that while it was natural for them to observe it, they would hardly have done so without their Lord's sanction — a sanction his repeated presence gave, so that from this time, Barnes says, the historical fact of the day's observance is indisputable, as Acts 20 and 1 Corinthians 16 and Revelation 1 show. Ellicott, the grammatical-historical voice, is more cautious. There is no reason to think they had not met during the interval, nor that this particular meeting was a special observance of the Lord's day; but he allows that an appearance falling on the recurrence of the first day would take its place among the steps by which the disciples passed from the Jewish sabbath to the Christian Sunday.

Lightfoot dissents from the reading most of the others take for granted. He would not easily believe, he says, that the evangelist's intention here was to tell us Christ penetrated the doors with his body; rather the doors were shut for fear of the Jews, as a week before, and the detail is repeated to let us know the disciples were still at Jerusalem, where their greatest danger lay — on the morrow, he supposes, they were to set out for Galilee. Robertson simply dates it, the next Sunday evening, counting inclusively as the phrase about three days is counted, and notes the scene is exactly that of the earlier appearance except that this time the twelfth man is there.

On the greeting, Ellicott hears two things at once. It is partly the natural salutation as he appears, now full of a new meaning that the thoughts of the week must have written on their hearts, and partly, he suggests, specially meant to take in the man who had not been there to hear it the first time.
