Chrysostom, the Eastern voice, puts the condescension plainly: because one person would examine him, Christ allowed it. Calvin, the reformed voice, draws the lesson from the readiness — when Christ so readily yields to an improper request, we learn how earnestly he labours to overcome unbelief.
27:
He is addressed by name, and the first thing every witness notices is that his private words have been overheard. Robertson sees the Lord turn directly to him as though he had come expressly for his sake, revealing his knowledge of the doubt and naming the very tests the man had set. Ellicott makes that knowledge the real argument: the repetition of the conditions implies that the words of the previous week were heard, which in itself would carry conviction — and, with the conviction, a sense of shame. Chrysostom, the Eastern voice, says he comes himself and does not wait to be interrogated, using the same words in order to show he had heard them, and divides the saying in two: first a rebuke, in the offered hands and side, and then an admonition.

Gill notices the manner rather than the matter. He singled out at once the man for whose sake he chiefly came, and called him by name in the most friendly way, without upbraiding or reproaching him for refusing the testimony given him. Clarke, the wesleyan-arminian, calls it infinite compassion, a condescension that accommodates itself to the prejudices of an obstinate though sincere disciple — and thinks it very probable the invitation was taken up, since an unbelief so deeply rooted was not easily cured.

Why the wounds were there to be touched at all is a question Chrysostom and Augustine both raise. We may wonder, Chrysostom says, how an incorruptible body could retain the marks of nails; and his answer is that it was done in condescension, so that they might be sure it was the very person who had been crucified. Augustine presses it further. He might, had he pleased, have wiped all spot and trace of wound from his glorified body, but he had reasons for keeping them: he showed them to the man who would not believe without seeing and touching, and he will show them one day to his enemies too, though not with the same words. Chrysostom adds an observation that covers the whole stretch of the chapter: before they receive the Holy Spirit their faith wavers, and afterwards it is firm.

The closing command is where Ellicott does his best work. He would render it become not unbelieving, but believing, and insists the words do not apply to the fact of the resurrection only but to the general spiritual condition of the man. He stood in danger of passing out of the state of a believer in Christ into that of an unbeliever; his demand for the evidence of the senses was a step backward, a resting on the less certain rather than the more; and his Master would have him retrace that step and come to rest instead on the intuition of the Spirit. Robertson reads the grammar the same way — a present imperative, stop becoming disbelieving — and notices the play between the two words, the unbelieving and the believing, that the sentence turns on. He adds the remark the verse has earned: the doubt, in the face of the witness of all the others, was no proof of superior intelligence, though sceptics commonly pose as men of unusual mentality.
28:
He never touches anything. Ellicott, the grammatical-historical voice, takes that to be implied: the tests his Master offered were not used, and he expressed the fulness of his conviction at once — which the next verse confirms, since what is commended there is having seen. Wesley traces the distance travelled in a sentence. The others had said they had seen the Lord; this man now not only acknowledges him as Lord, which he had done before, and as risen, which they had affirmed, but confesses his Godhead, and more explicitly than anyone had yet done — and all of it without putting his hand upon the side.

Whether the words are addressed to Christ or thrown upward as an exclamation is the one question here, and the witnesses close it from several directions. Ellicott notes that the confession is preceded by said unto him and followed by because thou hast seen me, so that the first title can only refer to Christ, and the sentence cannot be taken as an exclamation addressed to God without violence to the context. Robertson calls it address and not exclamation, a vocative, and observes that Jesus accepts the words and goes on to praise the man who said them. Clarke, the wesleyan-arminian, reports that those who deny the Godhead of Christ would have the words be an exclamation of surprise directed to the Father, names Theodore of Mopsuestia as the first he knows to read them so, and notes that the fifth ecumenical council at Constantinople anathematised him for it. A man must do violence to every rule of construction, Clarke says, to apply this address to any but Christ.

Barnes assembles the argument in full, and it is the most careful thing written on the verse. There is no evidence the words were a mere expression of surprise; the language was addressed to Jesus himself, the text saying expressly that he said it unto him; and the Saviour neither reproved nor checked him, which Barnes finds impossible to reconcile with his honesty had he not been divine, since no pious man would allow such language to be addressed to him — as the apostles in Acts 14 and the angel in Revelation 22 both refused it. More than that, the Saviour immediately commends him for believing, and this declaration is the only evidence of belief there is: if it were simply an outcry of astonishment, what proof of faith would it be, when a moment before he doubted? And if it were not meant as it stands, Barnes concludes, it was an act of profaneness, and Christ would hardly have commended a man for taking the name of the Lord his God in vain.

Clarke adds two observations the others miss. The first is what the words meant in the speaker's mouth: thou art the very same person, my Lord whose disciple I have so long been, and thou art my God, henceforth the object of my religious adoration — so that the first man to give Jesus the title of God was the man who had lately refused to believe him alive, and made some amends by it. The second is about the company. From this point forward, Clarke says, the whole body of the disciples treated their Lord with the most supreme respect, and never again used the familiarity they had often used before. He quotes Bishop Pearce to the same effect, that Jesus did not reprove the title though this was probably the first time he was called so, and then asks his own question: could he have been jealous for the honour of the true God, could he have been a prophet, could he have been even an honest man, and let a disciple rest in a mistake so monstrous, if a mistake were what it was?
29:
Two textual facts shape how this is heard. Clarke notes that the name in the opening clause is omitted by almost every manuscript, version and ancient commentator of importance; Ellicott says the same of all the better copies, and adds that the order of the remaining words suggests they be read as a question — because thou hast seen me, hast thou believed? The tense, he observes, is a perfect-present, so the question asks whether the man has become, and now is, a believer. Gill lists the copies where the name is missing — the Alexandrian, Beza's ancient copy and some others, together with the Syriac, Arabic and Ethiopic versions. Robertson, quoting Bernard, adds the detail that decides what kind of evidence did the work: it was sight and not touch that convinced him, since the offered test was never used.

Ellicott is careful about the tone. The command of the previous verse had done its work, and these are words of approval — yet not wholly so. He had come to conviction by means of the senses, whereas the higher blessedness belongs to those who see by the eye of the spirit rather than the body, resting their confidence on the faith-faculty and standing independent of the changing phenomena of sense. Robertson puts it more bluntly: the confession was noble, but he missed the highest form of faith, the sort without the evidence of the senses — and Robertson hears in 1 Peter 1 language that seems a reminiscence of these very words by a man who was in the room to hear them. Calvin, the reformed voice, keeps the blame narrow — Christ finds nothing in him to blame except that he was so slow to believe that he had to be drawn by the experience of the senses, which is at variance with the nature of faith itself.

On the beatitude Ellicott is precise about its reach. The truth is stated in its general form, and is not to be taken in any special sense of the ten, both because the Greek is against it and because the others had also seen before they believed; it takes in everyone who has become a believer without having seen. The blessedness is thought of as existing from the moment of believing, which is why the act of faith stands in the past tense — and the words look forward, Ellicott says, to the development of a church founded on apostolic witness, whose faith must always be in the unseen. Barnes reads the sentence as a benediction rather than a description, approving this man's faith while commending more highly the faith of those who would believe without having seen.

Clarke makes the application that the verse invites and does not hedge it. To believe in Jesus on the testimony of his apostles puts a man in possession of the very same blessedness the apostles themselves enjoyed; God has so constituted the whole economy of grace that a believer at eighteen hundred years' distance, as Clarke reckoned it, suffers no loss for never having seen Christ in the flesh. He turns to the reader directly at the end: Christ died for thee, believe, and become as blessed as an apostle.

Both Clarke and Lightfoot support the thought from the rabbis, and the saying is a good one. Rabbi Simeon ben Lachish held the proselyte more beloved of God than the whole crowd that stood before Sinai — for unless they had heard the thunderings and seen the flames and the lightnings, the hills trembling and the trumpets sounding, they would not have received the law; whereas the proselyte has seen none of it, and has come in all the same, devoting himself to God and taking the kingdom of heaven upon him.
30:
A writer stops and tells you how much he has left out, and the witnesses divide over how much that is. Clarke, the wesleyan-arminian, reads it narrowly: besides the two entries through shut doors already described, the other miracles not related here were such as were necessary to the disciples only, and so were not revealed to mankind at large. He makes a principle of it — there is nothing in the whole revelation of God but what serves some important purpose, and nothing left out that could have been of any real use. Ellicott, the grammatical-historical voice, reads it as wide as the life, and argues the point. There were not many other signs within the forty days; the phrase did Jesus does not suit the appearances to the disciples; and the words in this book refer to everything that has preceded. The signs, therefore, are the works wrought through the whole ministry, and the writer is explaining why he has recorded so little of a life that held so much — many things he remembered as an eyewitness simply fell outside his purpose.

Robertson agrees that the reference is broad, naming the signs alluded to in general terms earlier in this Gospel as well as those the other three record, and gives the grammar its force: a periphrastic perfect, so that they do not stand written in this book. He notes that the phrase for in the presence of the disciples is a common idiom in Luke, absent from Mark and Matthew, and used by John himself only once elsewhere. Barnes observes that many of the omitted works were recorded by the other evangelists and many never recorded at all, as the close of the following chapter says outright.

Ellicott draws the structural conclusion the verse invites. It would seem to follow, he says, that these two verses are the conclusion of the original Gospel, and that the chapter after them is to be regarded as a postscript or appendix — though he adds that there will be reason to believe the appendix came from the apostle's own hand. Augustine, the Latin voice, had made the same observation and turned it the other way. The paragraph indicates, as it were, the end of the book; and yet the manifestation at the sea of Tiberias is related afterwards, where the draught of fishes refers in a special way to the mystery of the Church as it will be in the final resurrection of the dead. Augustine thinks the interposed ending was fitted to give that narrative greater prominence, standing as a kind of preface to what follows rather than a door closed on it.

Calvin, the reformed voice, values the note for its honesty. Without it, readers might have supposed that the evangelist had left out none of the miracles and had given a full and complete account; as it stands, he testifies that he has related only some things out of a large number. Henry, the puritan-evangelical voice, keeps to the purpose rather than the arithmetic: there were other signs and other proofs of the resurrection, and these were committed to writing so that all might believe Jesus to be the promised Messiah and the Son of God, and by that faith obtain eternal life. Robertson ends where Henry does, observing that the book is written with a purpose, and that its author is about to state it.
31:
A book that has run to twenty chapters stops to say what it is for, and Ellicott, the grammatical-historical voice, reads the sentence as both a statement of object and an explanation of what looks like an abrupt ending. The object is that those for whom the author writes may become believers, and may read in the signs the spiritual truths lying behind them. Ellicott then traces what the Gospel has actually been doing: it has followed, step by step, the development of faith in the apostles themselves, and that development has reached its highest stage in the confession of the last doubter — after which the blessedness of those who will believe without sight is pronounced in the Master's own words. In that confession and that comment, he says, the author's object finds full expression, and with those words the Gospel finds its fitting close. The three sayings the writer had heard and set down — become not unbelieving but believing, my Lord and my God, blessed are they that have not seen and yet have believed — are the reason the record exists.

On the closing phrase Ellicott prefers life in his name to life through his name, and notices that the last words of the book bring the reader back to its first, where life and the right to be called children of God were already in view. He adds that the wording has a special point against the heresies current when it was written.

Robertson keeps to the tense and finds the whole history of the book in it. The subjunctive is present — that you may keep on believing — and he observes that the book has had precisely this effect of a continuous confirmation of faith. Barnes reads the verse as the clue to the design John had in view, namely to prove that Jesus was the Messiah, so that those who read might be convinced and have eternal life. Clarke, the wesleyan-arminian, states it in the same terms and adds the textual note that many copies read eternal life in the last clause: the Gospel is written to give full proof that Jesus is the promised Messiah, and that through him every believer might have that life.

Calvin, the reformed voice, reads the verse as a boundary set against a certain kind of appetite. The evangelist committed to writing what ought to satisfy us, because it is abundantly sufficient for confirming our faith, and in saying so he is answering the vain curiosity that always wants more than it has been given. Cyril of Jerusalem, the Eastern voice, fixes on the content of the confession rather than its sufficiency, pressing the clause that Jesus is the Christ against those who will allow the man and not the title. Wesley keeps to the order of the two clauses, belief first and life following from it.

What the witnesses agree on is the shape of the claim, and it is a modest one for a book making an immodest assertion. The record is selective and admits it; it is arranged toward a verdict rather than a biography; and the verdict it wants is the one a man who had refused all testimony reached when he stopped asking for proof. That is why the chapter can end here, with the writer's hand shown and his purpose named, and why he can leave so much out without apology.
